scenes.title: Amazon EC2
scenes.visual_overview: How an EC2 virtual server is assembled from an OS image, instance type, storage, network security and optional scaling.
visual_walkthrough: AMI as OS/software template
Instance type selects CPU/memory/accelerator
EC2 instance plus EBS block storage
Security group and scaling arrows lead to deployed app
Bottom request path for a custom AI inference model
EC2 versus SageMaker comparison
scenes.visual_example: A user requests an AI inference endpoint running custom model software on EC2 in a VPC; model files and logs are on EBS.
scenes.visual_synthesis: EC2 provides server control, while SageMaker manages more ML workflow infrastructure.
scenes.narration: This visual introduces Amazon EC2 as a cloud virtual server for applications you choose to install and run, including custom AI inference software. Follow the numbered journey in the top row. First choose an Amazon Machine Image, or AMI: the starting operating system and preconfigured software. Second select an instance type with appropriate CPU, memory or GPU resources. Third launch that EC2 virtual machine. From the instance, three related configuration paths branch right. EBS supplies persistent block storage for files and logs. A security group permits only required inbound and outbound connections. Scaling settings can add or remove instances when traffic changes. These are cooperating services and settings, not automatically bundled functionality of one server. The bottom-left diagram provides the concrete example: a user sends a request over the internet to an application running on EC2 inside a VPC; the instance loads the model and returns predictions or recommendations. The middle comparison explains the architectural decision: EC2 means you manage the operating environment, installed frameworks and application; SageMaker supplies more managed training, deployment and monitoring capabilities. The big-picture takeaway is to choose EC2 for customizable infrastructure when you accept the responsibility of configuring and operating it.

scenes.title: EC2 Sizing for AI Workloads
scenes.visual_overview: Choose server resources against model footprint, target latency and requests per second, then trace the load-balanced request path.
visual_walkthrough: CPU versus GPU choices with different model sizes and throughput
Memory capacity, serving headroom and workers
EBS persistent versus instance store temporary files
Network, VPC, load balancer and security-group gates
Client HTTPS to ELB to EC2 Auto Scaling group diagram with stored model files
Bottom large generative model scenario and requirements
scenes.visual_example: A several-billion-parameter inference service chooses GPU compute, enough RAM, EBS for model artifacts, an ALB and restricted incoming traffic.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Performance is end to end: compute, memory, storage, networking and permissions must meet workload requirements together.
scenes.narration: This slide teaches how to size an EC2 deployment for a model, rather than picking an instance type by its name. The top right identifies three drivers: model size, desired requests per second and latency target. Follow the five numbered panels. First choose CPU for suitable smaller or general workloads, or GPU where a large model and high throughput make acceleration worthwhile. Next make sure memory holds the model and serving overhead, including multiple workers or batches. The third panel separates EBS, which persists model artifacts and logs, from temporary high-performance instance store, which can be lost when the instance ends. Fourth, plan network bandwidth and placement in a VPC and subnet. Fifth, limit security-group inbound and outbound traffic to what is necessary. Now trace the large lower diagram: a client makes an HTTPS inference request to Elastic Load Balancing. The load balancer forwards to model servers in an Auto Scaling group, which load persistent model artifacts from EBS. The bottom worked example walks the same choices for a multi-billion-parameter generative model: GPU, memory headroom, persistent storage, sufficient network, and restrictive access from the load balancer. The whole system is only as fast and secure as its constrained component; benchmark performance rather than assuming a GPU is always the best choice.

scenes.title: EC2 User Data
scenes.visual_overview: An EC2 user-data script can bootstrap software during initial launch and produce a functioning web server.
visual_walkthrough: Four numbered top panels: choose AMI, add user-data script, run at first boot, application ready
Elevated root privileges on Linux at initial boot
Bottom Bash script: yum update/install nginx, systemctl enable/start, echo HTML
Browser example Hello from EC2
Safety panel: once by default, explicit reruns, keep secrets out, Parameter Store/Secrets Manager
scenes.visual_example: Linux user data installs nginx and writes an index page reading Hello from EC2 on the first boot.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Bootstrapping is not the same as proven application health, and user-data text must not contain secrets.
scenes.narration: This diagram shows how to prepare an EC2 instance automatically, without logging in to perform every installation by hand. Across the top, choose an AMI, provide a user-data script as you launch the server, and let the Linux first-boot process execute it with elevated privileges. The rightmost panel represents the intended ready application, but a launched instance should still be health-checked. Now inspect the real example at the bottom. The Bash header tells Linux how to run the commands. The script updates packages, installs nginx, enables it to start automatically, starts the service and writes a simple Hello from EC2 page to the web directory. The illustrated browser should then display that text if networking and the web server are correctly configured. The important-considerations panel adds the operating rules. Linux user-data scripts typically execute once on first launch by default; rerunning on every boot needs explicit configuration through cloud-init or another startup mechanism. Because the script can be visible to people with access to instance metadata or configuration, do not embed passwords or API keys. Use an authorized secrets retrieval service such as Systems Manager Parameter Store or Secrets Manager. The whole visual links infrastructure launch, first-boot configuration and application-readiness verification.

scenes.title: EC2 Launch Workflow
scenes.visual_overview: A six-step AWS console launch from image choice to network, storage, IAM and real connectivity checks.
visual_walkthrough: Six top stages from AMI and type to VPC/subnet/security, EBS/role/user data, launch, verify
Bottom concrete Amazon Linux t3.micro, 8-GiB gp3, role, bootstrap
Public access prerequisites: address, IGW route, group permissions, trusted SSH
Stop versus terminate comparison with EBS and instance store consequences
scenes.visual_example: Launch an Amazon Linux web server in a public subnet, install httpd from user data, test port 80 and restrict SSH to trusted addresses.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A running state alone does not prove public reachability; stopping preserves some resources, termination deletes the instance.
scenes.narration: This slide gives an end-to-end EC2 launch checklist and then contrasts stopping with terminating the instance. Follow the six top panels in order. Select an Amazon Linux, Ubuntu or Windows AMI; select an instance family and size; choose the VPC, subnet and security group; configure EBS volumes, an optional IAM role and user data; review and launch; then verify instance health and connect using a suitable method. The lower example makes the choices concrete: Amazon Linux, a t3.micro instance, a public subnet, an eight-gibibyte gp3 root volume and a web-server bootstrap script that installs and starts httpd. A green running status is only one check. For an internet client to reach HTTP, the instance needs a public address, a suitable route through an internet gateway and traffic permitted by relevant controls; SSH or RDP should be restricted to trusted source addresses. Now compare the two right-side boxes. Stopping an EBS-backed instance allows restart and generally preserves attached EBS volumes, but instance-store data is lost. Termination removes the instance; the root EBS volume is normally deleted by default, while each extra volume follows its DeleteOnTermination setting. This distinction matters for troubleshooting, data retention and costs after shutdown.
